citing_sentences: Despite the remarkable success of Zero-shot-CoT in solving multi-step reasoning tasks, its results on a sample of $100$ arithmetic test examples still point to three pitfalls (as shown in Figure 1): (i) Calculation errors (in $7\%$ of test examples): These are errors in the calculation leading to wrong answers; (ii) Missing Step errors (in $12\%$ of test examples): These occur when some intermediate reasoning step(s) is missed-out especially when there are many steps involved; (iii) Semantic misunderstanding (in $27\%$ of test examples): There are other errors in semantic understanding of the problem and coherence of reasoning steps likely to be caused by the insufficient capability of LLMs.

abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have recently been shown to deliver impressive performance in various NLP tasks. To tackle multi-step reasoning tasks, few-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting includes a few manually crafted step-by-step reasoning demonstrations which enable LLMs to explicitly generate reasoning steps and improve their reasoning task accuracy. To eliminate the manual effort, Zero-shot-CoT concatenates the target problem statement with “Let’s think step by step” as an input prompt to LLMs. Despite the success of Zero-shot-CoT, it still suffers from three pitfalls: calculation errors, missing-step errors, and semantic misunderstanding errors. To address the missing-step errors, we propose Plan-and-Solve (PS) Prompting. It consists of two components: first, devising a plan to divide the entire task into smaller subtasks, and then carrying out the subtasks according to the plan. To address the calculation errors and improve the quality of generated reasoning steps, we extend PS prompting with more detailed instructions and derive PS+ prompting. We evaluate our proposed prompting strategy on ten datasets across three reasoning problems. The experimental results over GPT-3 show that our proposed zero-shot prompting consistently outperforms Zero-shot-CoT across all datasets by a large margin, is comparable to or exceeds Zero-shot-Program-of-Thought Prompting, and has comparable performance with 8-shot CoT prompting on the math reasoning problem. The code can be found at https://github.com/AGI-Edgerunners/Plan-and-Solve-Prompting.

sections.body: The paper analyses errors from Zero-shot-CoT on a sample of 100 arithmetic test examples. It reports three error types: calculation errors in 7% of examples, missing-step errors in 12%, and semantic misunderstanding errors in 27%. To address missing steps, the authors propose Plan-and-Solve (PS) prompting, which asks the model to devise a plan and then carry it out. PS+ adds instructions to extract variables and calculate intermediate results, aimed at calculation errors. The paper evaluates these prompts on six arithmetic, two commonsense, and two symbolic datasets.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Zero-shot chain-of-thought errors are split into calculation, missing-step, and semantic errors, and a plan-based prompt targets two of them.

sections.body: PS prompting replaces the Zero-shot-CoT trigger with an instruction to first understand the problem and devise a plan, then carry out the plan step by step. PS+ adds the instructions to extract relevant variables and their corresponding numerals, to pay attention to calculation, and to calculate intermediate results. Step 1 generates the reasoning and answer with greedy decoding. Step 2 appends a prompt such as "Therefore, the answer (arabic numerals) is" to extract the final number from that reasoning text. No demonstration examples are used.
sections.heading: Plan-and-Solve Prompting
sections.headline: Plan-and-Solve prompting uses a zero-shot trigger that asks the model to devise and carry out a plan, followed by an answer-extraction prompt.

sections.body: The benchmarks cover six arithmetic datasets (GSM8K, SVAMP, MultiArith, AddSub, AQUA, SingleEq), two commonsense datasets (CSQA and StrategyQA), and two symbolic datasets (Last Letter Concatenation and Coin Flip). Baselines are Zero-shot-CoT, zero-shot PoT, Manual-CoT with eight hand-crafted demonstrations, and Auto-CoT. Decoding uses temperature 0. Evaluation reports accuracy. The paper states that the GPT-3 175B model is used as the backbone.
sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.headline: Experiments use ten benchmarks with text-davinci-003 and compare against zero-shot and few-shot baselines.

sections.body: In Table 2, PS+ improves on Zero-shot-CoT by at least 5% on all arithmetic datasets except GSM8K, where the gain is 2.9%. PS+ averages 76.7, compared with 70.4 for Zero-shot-CoT and 77.6 for Manual-CoT. On commonsense tasks, PS+ reaches 71.9 on CSQA and 65.4 on StrategyQA, against 65.2 and 63.8 for Zero-shot-CoT. On symbolic tasks, PS+ reaches 75.2 on Last Letter and 99.6 on Coin Flip. The authors note that the comparison with few-shot methods is unfair. Self-consistency with N set to 10 raises GSM8K to 73.7 and SVAMP to 84.4.
sections.heading: Experimental Results
sections.headline: PS+ outperforms Zero-shot-CoT on all arithmetic datasets and averages 76.7 against 77.6 for Manual-CoT.

sections.body: The section groups prior work on reasoning in NLP and on prompting. It describes Chain-of-Thought prompting, Program-of-Thought prompting, Zero-shot-CoT, and Auto-CoT. The authors state that their approach differs from these by eliciting multi-step reasoning zero-shot. Their method asks the LLM to write a plan that decomposes the task, and it adds detailed instructions to avoid obvious reasoning errors. The section cites a survey for further related work.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work places Plan-and-Solve among chain-of-thought methods that use zero-shot prompting and planning.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the three error types found in Zero-shot-CoT and the two PS variants that target them. Across all evaluated datasets, PS+ outperforms previous zero-shot baselines and performs on par with few-shot CoT on several arithmetic datasets. The authors suggest that PS prompting could extend to non-reasoning tasks and that refining the plan is a direction for future work.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The authors conclude that plan-based zero-shot prompting outperforms Zero-shot-CoT and matches few-shot CoT on some arithmetic datasets.

sections.body: The authors state two limitations. First, designing prompts that guide the model to generate correct reasoning takes effort, and GPT-3 is sensitive to prompt wording. Second, PS prompting reduces calculation and missing-step errors, but semantic misunderstanding errors remain. The authors say they plan to address semantic errors through prompting rather than by upgrading the LLM.
sections.heading: Limitations
sections.headline: Prompt design is labour-intensive and the method does not address semantic misunderstanding errors.

sections.body: The section names the six math, two commonsense, and two symbolic datasets used. It records the licences that the authors list for GSM8K, SVAMP, AQUA, and StrategyQA, and notes that the licences of the remaining datasets are unspecified. The authors state that the prompts do not collect or use personal information and contain no words that discriminate against any individual or group. They also state that the prompts would not negatively affect other people's safety.
sections.heading: Ethics
sections.headline: The paper lists the datasets and their licences and states that the prompts contain no personal information or discriminatory wording.

sections.body: Tables 7 to 16 report accuracy for each trigger sentence tried on AQuA, GSM8K, MultiArith, SVAMP, AddSub, SingleEq, CSQA, StrategyQA, Last Letters, and Coin Flip. Tables 17 to 26 show example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+ for each dataset. The main text states that the authors used GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) for these experiments.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: Appendix lists trigger-sentence ablations for every dataset and example outputs from Zero-shot-PS+.
